subject: mathematics
title: Understand fractions, decimals and percentages
promise: This starts from the very beginning: fractions, decimals and percentages are the SAME numbers wearing three different outfits. Once you can change one outfit into another, every question in this topic gets easier.

sections.heading: One number, three outfits
sections.body:
Here is the idea the whole topic rests on: a fraction, a decimal and a percentage can all describe exactly the same amount.
Half of something can be written as the fraction 1/2, as the decimal 0.5, or as the percentage 50%. Three different costumes — one number underneath.
Every skill in this topic is really just one skill: changing a number from one costume into another, and picking the costume that makes the question easiest.
sections.example: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. Say it out loud: one half, nought point five, fifty per cent — all the same amount.

sections.heading: What a decimal actually says
sections.body:
The digits after a decimal point are pieces of a whole, and their position tells you the size of the pieces. The first place after the point counts TENTHS. The second place counts HUNDREDTHS.
So 0.3 means 3 tenths — the fraction 3/10. And 0.07 means 7 hundredths — the fraction 7/100. Put together, 0.37 means 3 tenths and 7 hundredths, which is 37 hundredths in total: 37/100.
A decimal is not a mysterious new thing. It is a fraction whose bottom number is 10 or 100, written without the fraction bar.
sections.example: 0.9 = 9/10. And 0.45 = 45/100, which is 4 tenths and 5 hundredths.

sections.heading: From fractions to decimals
sections.body:
If a fraction's bottom number is 10 or 100, it slides straight into decimal form: 7/10 = 0.7, and 23/100 = 0.23.
For other friendly fractions, first change them into tenths or hundredths using equivalent fractions. 1/2 = 5/10 = 0.5. And 1/5 = 2/10 = 0.2, because multiplying top and bottom by 2 keeps the fraction the same. 3/4 = 75/100 = 0.75, because multiplying top and bottom by 25 turns quarters into hundredths.
Keep this rule close: whatever you multiply the bottom by, you must multiply the top by too.
sections.example: 2/5 = 4/10 = 0.4. Top and bottom were both multiplied by 2.

sections.heading: Between decimals and percentages
sections.body:
Per cent means out of every 100, so a percentage is a count of hundredths. 45% is 45 hundredths — the decimal 0.45. And 0.7 is 70 hundredths — which is 70%.
So to go from a decimal to a percentage, ask: how many hundredths is this? 0.09 is 9 hundredths, so it is 9% — not 90%. The zero right after the point matters.
To go from a percentage to a decimal, do the reverse: 30% is 30 hundredths, which is 0.30, usually written 0.3.
sections.example: 0.65 = 65%. 8% = 0.08. Watch the small ones: 0.05 is 5%, not 50%.

sections.heading: Comparing and ordering the three forms
sections.body:
Which is biggest: 0.6, 55%, or 1/2? You cannot compare numbers while they are wearing different costumes. The trick is to change them all into the SAME costume first — percentages usually work best, because they are plain whole numbers out of 100.
0.6 is 60%. 55% stays 55%. 1/2 is 50%. Now it is easy: 60% is the biggest, so 0.6 wins.
This one move — convert everything, then compare — turns every ordering question into a question about whole numbers.
sections.example: Order 3/4, 0.7 and 72% from smallest to largest: they become 75%, 70% and 72%, so the order is 0.7, then 72%, then 3/4.

sections.heading: Finding a percentage of an amount: the 10% building block
sections.body:
To find a percentage of an amount, start with the easiest block: 10%. Because 10% is one tenth, you find it by dividing by 10. 10% of 60 is 6.
Now build. 30% is three blocks of 10%: for 30% of 60, take 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. 5% is half a block: 5% of 80 is half of 8, which is 4. And 15%? One block plus half a block: 15% of 60 is 6 + 3 = 9.
With 10%, 5% and 1% (divide by 100), you can build almost any percentage a question asks for.

mistakes.right: 0.5 is 50%. It is 5 TENTHS, which is 50 hundredths.
mistakes.why: A percentage counts hundredths, but the first decimal place counts tenths — each tenth is worth 10 hundredths.
The 5 in 1/5 is a piece COUNT, not a percentage. Change the fraction into hundredths before you read off a per cent.

mistakes.wrong: Comparing 0.8 and 45% and picking 45% because 45 is bigger than 8.
mistakes.why: Never compare numbers in different costumes. Convert both to the same form first, then compare.

check.question: Which percentage is the same as 0.7?
Which decimal is the same as 3/10?
check.explanation: The first place after the decimal point counts tenths, so 3 tenths is 0.3.

check.question: Write 45% as a decimal.
check.explanation: 45% is 45 hundredths, and 45 hundredths is written 0.45.

check.question: Which percentage is the same as 1/5?
check.explanation: 1/5 = 2/10 = 20/100 = 20%. The 5 counts pieces, it is not the percentage.

check.question: Which is the LARGEST: 0.6, 55%, or 1/2?
check.explanation: Convert to one costume: 0.6 = 60%, and 1/2 = 50%. 60% beats 55% and 50%.

check.question: What is 30% of 60?
check.explanation: 10% of 60 is 6, and 30% is three of those blocks: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18.

check.question: Which decimal is the same as 3/4?
check.explanation: 3/4 = 75/100 (multiply top and bottom by 25), and 75 hundredths is 0.75.

check.question: What is 5% of 80?
check.explanation: 10% of 80 is 8, and 5% is half of that: 4.

check.question: Which percentage is the same as 0.09?
check.explanation: 0.09 is 9 hundredths — 9%. The zero after the point means there are no tenths.

check.question: Which percentage is the same as 2/5?

practice.hint: 25% is a quarter — halve 44, then halve again.
0.4 is 4 tenths — how many hundredths is that?
Find 10% first, then take three blocks of it.
15% is one 10% block plus half a block: 6 + 3.

practice.prompt: Write 0.35 as a fraction out of 100.

practice.hint: Change all three into percentages, then compare: 70%, 65% and 75%.
10% of 260 is 26. 5% is half of that.
